Watches of Switzerland London to host GPHG winners in first public showcase

London watch fans can see the 2026 GPHG winners up close at Watches of Switzerland’s Knightsbridge showroom this November.

BY

Karen Carillo
10th Sep 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:13
Instaread

The GPHG awards usually wrap up with trophies being handed out in Geneva, but this November the celebration will carry on in London. Collectors there will get their own chance to see the winning watches in person.

Just days after the ceremony, Watches of Switzerland will bring the 2026 Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève winners to its Knightsbridge showroom from November 19 to 23. It will be the first public exhibition in London of this year’s winning watches, following three similar showcases hosted by the retailer in the US.

The winners are coming straight from Geneva

The exhibition takes place less than two weeks after the GPHG awards ceremony on November 7. The annual event has been running since 2001 and recognises watches across categories covering everything from complications and jewellery to artistic crafts.

The actual winners are still to be decided. This year, 20 prizes will be handed out, including the Aiguille d’Or Grand Prix, the competition’s top honour. A 24-person jury will help choose the winners alongside votes from the GPHG Academy, which includes more than 1,000 members from the watch industry and related fields.

Advertisement

That makes the Knightsbridge exhibition a useful second act to the ceremony. Photos and specifications can only show so much, especially when some of the winning pieces are recognised for finishing, movement architecture, gem-setting or decorative work that can be easier to appreciate in person.

Visitors will also be able to see the winners together instead of tracking them down through individual brand boutiques and exhibitions.

Watches of Switzerland has done this before in the US

Although this will be a first for the retailer in London, Watches of Switzerland already has experience hosting GPHG winners. It has staged exhibitions of award-winning watches in the US on three previous occasions.

Knightsbridge gives the exhibition a suitably prominent London setting. The showroom at 47-51 Brompton Road stretches across three floors, carries a wide range of major watch brands and includes dedicated space for events and private appointments.

The exhibition begins with an invitation-only preview on Wednesday, November 18, before opening to the public the following day. The public run continues until Monday, November 23.

Specific exhibition opening hours have not yet been confirmed, so anyone planning a visit will need to check closer to the date.

Advertisement

London gets a closer look at the winners

The London exhibition gives enthusiasts who were not in Geneva a chance to get close to the watches soon after the results are announced.

There is also a nice timing element to it. By November 19, the conversation around which brands won, which watches missed out and what deserved the Aiguille d’Or will still be fresh. London visitors will then have the chance to judge some of those choices from a few inches away.

Watches of Switzerland says the exhibition is intended to give collectors and enthusiasts a closer look at the craftsmanship and ideas shaping contemporary watchmaking.

For anyone who usually follows the GPHG results from a screen, that may be the real draw. This time, some of the year’s most celebrated watches will be together in Knightsbridge, and the public can simply walk in and see them for themselves.

Tiffany’s new rope watch contains over 32 carats of diamonds

Tiffany & Co. has turned its Rope watch into a one-off platinum piece with over 32 carats of diamonds and nearly 12 carats of aquamarines.

BY

Karen Carillo
11th Sep 2026

Calling Tiffany & Co.’s latest Rope creation a watch almost undersells it. In fact, there are more than 44 carats of diamonds and aquamarines wrapped around the case, dial, bracelet and buckle before you even get to the timekeeping.

At the centre is a 37mm platinum case crossed by an 18k yellow-gold rope motif inspired by Jean Schlumberger’s archival designs. Tiffany will make just one example, giving the Rope concept a much more extravagant high-jewellery treatment.

More than 32 carats of diamonds cover the watch

The case itself forms a flower-like arrangement of 32 petals, each set with trapezoid-cut diamonds. Those stones total 10.38 carats and surround a fully pavé-set centre dial.

Tiffany has filled that dial with 40 trapezoid-cut aquamarines weighing another 1.61 carats. Against all that blue, the polished yellow-gold rope detail adds a warmer contrast and helps connect the watch with the wider Tiffany Rope collection.

The bracelet carries even more stones. Its links are set with 108 baguette-cut diamonds totalling 19.94 carats and 56 baguette aquamarines weighing 9.83 carats. Another 14 baguette diamonds and five aquamarines appear on the buckle.

Advertisement

Opinion

I’ve seen countless high-jewellery watches over the years, and they all tend to err on the side of being too wacky for any normal use. Impressive, sure, but you wouldn’t be seen dead in it, even at your most suave function.

This one, though, looks quite wearable, despite looking like something carved from the wall of a mine. Hats off to the team at Tiffany!

Sam Cross

Put everything together and Tiffany says the watch contains 154 baguette and trapezoid-cut diamonds totalling more than 32 carats, alongside 106 aquamarines approaching 12 carats.

With that many diamonds and aquamarines packed into the watch, the setting process is understandably time-consuming. Tiffany says crafting the piece and setting the stones by hand takes more than 120 hours.

The design goes back to Jean Schlumberger

The rope motif has deep roots at Tiffany. Schlumberger was known for turning twisted strands of gold into highly sculptural jewellery, and Tiffany’s archives include Rope pieces dating back to the early 1950s.

One of those archival designs is particularly relevant here: an 18k gold brooch set with diamonds and rubies around a prominent aquamarine. The new watch picks up that same contrast between rich gold, colourless diamonds and blue stone, then spreads it over an entire timepiece.

Tiffany has continued developing Rope into a broader jewellery and watch collection, with current models using twisted yellow-gold bezels and Swiss-made movements.

Advertisement

Here, Tiffany trades the smaller round diamonds of the standard models for baguette and trapezoid-cut stones.

Tiffany lets the gemstones do the talking

For all the complexity on the outside, the actual timekeeping is uncomplicated. The watch uses a high-precision Swiss quartz movement showing only the hours and minutes.

That may sound modest next to the gem-setting, but the emphasis here is clearly on jewellery rather than mechanical spectacle. Tiffany has treated the 37mm case, dial and bracelet as one continuous gemstone composition, with the movement largely staying out of the way.

Tiffany has also made just one example of the aquamarine Rope High Jewelry watch, that’s why this particular version is a true one-off.

With more than 44 carats of diamonds and aquamarines combined, it is a considerable step beyond the everyday Rope watches already in Tiffany’s collection. The basic twisted-gold idea remains, but almost every available surface around it has been handed over to gemstones.
